raw_response:
I will mostly do what worked for me last year, then adjust a little. I have 18 mu, so I cannot farm too loose. I still need steady grain from wheat and maize, because that is the base, and then I keep some cash crops for money in hand. Around here, if fertilizer is short, yield drops fast, and that hurts more than spending a bit extra, so I will not cut fertilizer too hard. But I also will not throw money around. I have well water, so I can push the better land a bit more on cabbage and eggplant.

For wheat and maize, I will keep the main area because that is the safest. I will put 12 mu into the wheat-maize rotation, same as the better years. On wheat, I will use improved seed, not old saved seed, because I have seen cleaner stands and better ears from that. I will give enough base fertilizer and topdress nitrogen once the wheat turns green strong. On maize after wheat, I will use hybrid seed. In my area, neighbors using hybrid maize usually get fuller cobs, so I will follow that. I will feed maize a little heavier than wheat, because if maize is hungry in summer, it shows fast.

For cabbage and eggplant, I will keep smaller plots because they need more watching, more spraying, and more picking. I will put 2 mu to cabbage and 2 mu to eggplant. Cabbage eats fertilizer and water, so I will feed it heavier and irrigate more times. Eggplant also needs steady water and spray work, but if managed well it brings cash over a longer picking period. For stevia, I will keep 2 mu as a side cash crop. I will not go big on it, because the market and management are less steady for me than grain. I will fertilize it enough to keep leaf growth good, but not as heavy as cabbage.

I will plough for wheat and most vegetables where I want a cleaner seedbed, and I will use rotary tillage after wheat for maize to save time. I do what I have seen work nearby: grain steady, vegetables for cash, and not too much risk on one crop.
